rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Among the following outermost electronic configurations of transition metals, which one shows the highest oxidation state ?
rows.solution:
The configuration showing the highest oxidation state is \(3d^5\,4s^2\).

Identify each element first. \(3d^6 4s^2\) is iron, \(3d^5 4s^1\) is chromium, \(3d^5 4s^2\) is MANGANESE and \(3d^3 4s^2\) is vanadium.

The highest oxidation state a transition metal reaches is the sum of its \(ns\) and unpaired \((n-1)d\) electrons — all of them available for bonding. Manganese has five unpaired d electrons plus two \(4s\) electrons, giving \(5 + 2 = 7\), and it does reach \(+7\), in the permanganate ion.

Chromium comes closest with \(5 + 1 = 6\), reached in the dichromate ion. Vanadium manages \(+5\), and iron, whose d electrons are no longer all unpaired, does not reach anything like \(+8\) in ordinary chemistry.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Which of the following solution in water will have the lowest freezing point ?
rows.solution:
The LOWEST freezing point belongs to the 1% CALCIUM CHLORIDE solution.

Depression of freezing point is a colligative property, so the solution with the MOST particles freezes lowest. Each solution here holds 1 g of solute, so compare moles of particles per gram.

Calcium chloride dissociates into THREE ions from a molar mass of 111, giving \(3/111 = 0{\cdot}027\). Potassium chloride gives two ions from 74.5, so \(2/74{\cdot}5 = 0{\cdot}0268\) — very close, but just behind. Urea gives \(1/60 = 0{\cdot}0167\) and glucose only \(1/180 = 0{\cdot}0056\).

The two non-electrolytes are easily eliminated; the real contest is between the two salts, and calcium chloride wins on the extra ion.

rows.stem:
Kohlrausch gave the following relation for strong electrolytes :
\(\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^{\circ} - \mathrm{A}\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\)
Which of the following equality holds true ?
rows.solution:
The equality holds as \(\mathrm{C} \longrightarrow 0\).

Read the relation itself. In \(\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^{\circ} - \mathrm{A}\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\), the term \(\mathrm{A}\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\) is what the measured molar conductivity falls short by, and it vanishes only when the concentration vanishes.

The chemistry behind the algebra: at any finite concentration the ions are close enough to interact with one another and to drag each other back, so they move more slowly than they otherwise would. Dilution moves them apart. At INFINITE DILUTION they are so far apart that they move entirely independently, and that limiting value is what \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) means.

Infinite dilution cannot be reached in a flask, which is why the relation matters: for a STRONG electrolyte it lets \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) be found by plotting \(\Lambda_m\) against \(\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\) and extrapolating the straight line back to zero.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: Unit of rate constant ‘k’ for a second order reaction is :
rows.solution:
The unit of the rate constant for a second order reaction is \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}\ L\ s^{-1}}\).

Derive it rather than remembering it. Rate always carries the units of concentration divided by time, \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\), and for order \(n\)
\(k = \dfrac{\text{Rate}}{[\mathrm{A}]^n}\)

Dividing by concentration \(n\) times gives the general form \(\mathrm{mol^{1-n}\ L^{n-1}\ s^{-1}}\). Put \(n = 2\):
\(\mathrm{mol^{-1}\ L\ s^{-1}}\)

The same formula gives \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\) for zero order — the same as rate — and \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) for first order, which is why the units alone identify the order.

rows.stem: The number of moles of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) precipitated when excess \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution is mixed with one mole of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]Cl}\) is :
rows.solution:
ONE mole of silver chloride is precipitated.

Silver nitrate precipitates only the chloride that is FREE IN SOLUTION, that is the counter ions outside the coordination sphere. In \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]Cl}\) the square brackets enclose two of the three chlorines: those two are LIGANDS, bonded directly to cobalt, and do not ionise. Only the third, written outside the brackets, is a counter ion.

Check the charges: four ammonia molecules are neutral and two chlorido ligands give \(-2\), so with cobalt at \(+3\) the complex ion is \(+1\) — balanced by exactly one chloride outside.

What is precipitated counts what is OUTSIDE the brackets, never the total chlorine in the formula. Written as \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4]Cl_3}\) the same atoms would give 3 mol; as \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_3]}\) they would give none.

rows.stem: The synthesis of alkyl fluoride is best carried out by :
rows.solution:
An alkyl fluoride is best made by the SWARTS REACTION.

An alkyl chloride or bromide is heated with a metallic fluoride — antimony trifluoride, or the fluorides of mercury(I), cobalt(II) or silver(I) — and the halogen is exchanged:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}Br} + \mathrm{AgF} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3{-}F} + \mathrm{AgBr}\)

The direct route is avoided because fluorine itself reacts with hydrocarbons far too violently to control.

Finkelstein is the same idea for IODIDES, using sodium iodide in dry acetone — and it works there because sodium chloride and bromide are insoluble in acetone while sodium iodide is soluble, so the equilibrium is pulled across. Sandmeyer replaces a diazonium group, and Wurtz couples two alkyl halides.

rows.stem: In the reaction \(\mathrm{R-OH} + \mathrm{HCl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{ZnCl_2}} \mathrm{RCl} + \mathrm{H_2O}\), what is the correct order of reactivity of alcohols ?
rows.solution:
The order of reactivity is \(1^{\circ} < 2^{\circ} < 3^{\circ}\) — tertiary alcohols react fastest.

This is the Lucas test, and it proceeds by the UNIMOLECULAR route. Zinc chloride, a Lewis acid, helps the protonated hydroxyl leave as water, and the carbocation left behind then picks up chloride.

Since the slow step is forming that carbocation, the reactivity follows carbocation STABILITY. A tertiary cation is stabilised by three alkyl groups releasing electron density towards it, a secondary by two, a primary by only one — so the order runs the way it does.

In practice a tertiary alcohol turns the reagent cloudy at once, a secondary one in about five minutes, and a primary one not at all without heating, which is what makes this a three way test.

rows.stem: Phenol reacts with Bromine \((\mathrm{Br_2})\) water to form :
rows.solution:
Phenol with BROMINE WATER gives 2,4,6-TRIBROMOPHENOL, as a white precipitate.

All three available positions are substituted at once, and no catalyst is needed. The hydroxyl group is so strongly activating — its lone pair is fed into the ring, raising the electron density most at the ortho and para positions — that even the feeble electrophile present in bromine water suffices. Water helps further by letting the phenol ionise to phenoxide, which is more strongly activating still.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + 3\mathrm{Br_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_2Br_3OH} + 3\mathrm{HBr}\)

The MONObromo products are what a non-polar solvent gives: bromine in carbon disulphide at low temperature stops after one substitution and yields a mixture of the ortho and para isomers. Same reagent, same substrate — the medium decides.

rows.stem: When excess of alkyl iodide is treated with ammonia, the product obtained is :
rows.solution:
With an EXCESS OF ALKYL IODIDE the product is A MIXTURE OF AMINES.

The trouble with this reaction is that it does not stop. Ammonia attacks the alkyl halide to give a primary amine, but that amine is a BETTER nucleophile than ammonia was, so it attacks another halide molecule to give the secondary amine, and that in turn gives the tertiary amine and finally the quaternary ammonium salt.

With the halide in excess there is no shortage of it at any stage, so every step proceeds and the product is a mixture — running on, if the excess is large enough, to the quaternary salt.

The opposite condition is what isolates a single product: a LARGE EXCESS OF AMMONIA makes any given halide molecule overwhelmingly likely to meet ammonia rather than an amine, so the PRIMARY amine dominates.

rows.stem: An amine ‘X’ reacts with Hinsberg reagent and the product obtained is insoluble in alkali. The amine ‘X’ is :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — option (D) alone is printed as a DRAWN structure: a benzene ring bonded to \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\). NAMED, not described: reading it as \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-NH_2}\) is lossless and does NOT state the answer, because the answer is option (A) and the discrimination the question tests (primary vs secondary vs tertiary vs aromatic) survives intact — options (A), (B) and (C) are already printed as formulas. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The amine is DIMETHYLAMINE, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}\).

Hinsberg's reagent is benzenesulphonyl chloride, and the test turns on how many hydrogens remain on the nitrogen after it reacts.

A SECONDARY amine gives a sulphonamide with NO hydrogen left on its nitrogen — both positions are now taken, one by each methyl group and one by the sulphonyl group. With no acidic hydrogen there is nothing for alkali to remove, so the product is INSOLUBLE in alkali, which is what the question describes.

A PRIMARY amine would leave one hydrogen on the nitrogen, made acidic by the two electron-withdrawing oxygens beside it, so its product DISSOLVES in alkali — that rules out both ethylamine and aniline. A TERTIARY amine has no nitrogen-hydrogen bond at all and does not react in the first place, so trimethylamine gives no product to test.

rows.stem: ‘Scurvy’ is caused due to the deficiency of :
rows.solution:
Scurvy is caused by a deficiency of VITAMIN C, ascorbic acid.

Vitamin C is needed to make collagen, the protein that holds connective tissue together, so without it the gums bleed, wounds fail to heal and the teeth loosen. It is WATER SOLUBLE, so the body cannot store it and a supply is needed regularly — which is why the disease appeared on long sea voyages and was cured by citrus fruit.

Of the others: vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, vitamin \(\mathrm{B_2}\) deficiency causes cheilosis, and vitamin D deficiency causes rickets.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : A mixture of \(o\)-nitrophenol and \(p\)-nitrophenol can be separated by steam distillation.
Reason (R) : \(o\)-nitrophenol is steam volatile due to intramolecular hydrogen bonding.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

In o-nitrophenol the nitro group and the hydroxyl group are close enough to bond to each other WITHIN the same molecule — intramolecular hydrogen bonding, sometimes called chelation. That uses up the hydroxyl's bonding capacity, so the molecules do not associate with one another, and the compound is volatile enough to distil over with the steam.

In p-nitrophenol the two groups are too far apart to reach each other, so the hydrogen bonding is INTERMOLECULAR: the molecules associate into larger aggregates, the compound is far less volatile, and it stays behind in the flask.

That difference in volatility is exactly what steam distillation exploits, so the Reason accounts for the Assertion completely.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Cooking time is reduced in pressure cooker.
Reason (R) : Boiling point of water inside the pressure cooker is lowered down.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Cooking time is indeed reduced in a pressure cooker. But the Reason has the effect backwards: the boiling point of the water inside is RAISED, not lowered.

A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the pressure on it. The cooker traps the steam and raises that pressure, so the water must be hotter than \(100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) before it can boil. The food is therefore cooked at a HIGHER temperature, reaction rates rise sharply with temperature, and the cooking finishes sooner.

The Reason, corrected, would have explained the Assertion; as written it would predict slower cooking, not faster. The genuinely lowered boiling point is what happens on a mountain, where the pressure is less and cooking takes longer.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Actinoids show irregularities in their electronic configurations.
Reason (R) : This is due to varying stability of \(\mathrm{f^0}\), \(\mathrm{f^7}\) and \(\mathrm{f^{14}}\) configurations.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

The actinoids do show irregular electronic configurations — thorium, protactinium, uranium and several others do not follow the pattern a simple filling order would predict.

And the cause is what the Reason gives. An EMPTY, HALF-FILLED or COMPLETELY FILLED f subshell — \(f^0\), \(f^7\), \(f^{14}\) — carries extra stability, so an electron will sometimes go into a \(6d\) orbital instead of a \(5f\) one in order to reach or keep such an arrangement. The two sets of orbitals lie close enough in energy for that small advantage to decide the matter.

The same effect appears in the first transition series, where chromium is \(3d^5 4s^1\) and copper \(3d^{10}4s^1\) rather than the expected \(4s^2\) configurations.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Maltose is a reducing sugar.
Reason (R) : One of the two glucose units can open to expose free aldehydic group in solution.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

A sugar is REDUCING if it can present a free aldehyde group to Tollens' or Fehling's reagent. Maltose is two glucose units joined by a glycosidic link between \(\mathrm{C_1}\) of the first and \(\mathrm{C_4}\) of the second — which leaves the SECOND unit's \(\mathrm{C_1}\), its anomeric carbon, untouched.

A free anomeric carbon can open back to the straight-chain form in solution, exposing an aldehyde group, and that is what reduces the reagent. So the Reason names precisely the mechanism the Assertion depends on.

The contrast is SUCROSE, where the link runs between the anomeric carbons of BOTH units. Neither ring can open, no aldehyde is ever exposed, and sucrose is non-reducing.

rows.stem: What is meant by negative deviation from Raoult’s law ? Give an example. What type of azeotrope is formed by negative deviation ?
rows.solution:
NEGATIVE DEVIATION from Raoult's law means the observed vapour pressure of the solution is LOWER than the value Raoult's law predicts from the mole fractions:
\(p_1 < p_1^{\,\circ}x_1\) and \(p_2 < p_2^{\,\circ}x_2\)

Why it happens. The interactions between UNLIKE molecules in the solution are STRONGER than those between the like molecules of each pure liquid. Held more tightly, the molecules escape into the vapour less readily than expected. Mixing is exothermic and the volume contracts slightly — the same fact seen from two other directions.

EXAMPLE: a solution of chloroform and acetone. Neither liquid hydrogen bonds to itself, but mixing them creates a new hydrogen bond — the chloroform hydrogen, made acidic by its three chlorines, bonds to the lone pair on the acetone oxygen. Nitric acid with water serves equally well.

TYPE OF AZEOTROPE: a MAXIMUM BOILING azeotrope. A lower vapour pressure means a higher boiling point, so the mixture at that composition boils ABOVE either pure component. Nitric acid and water form one at about 68% acid, boiling at \(393{\cdot}5\) K.

rows.stem: Write two differences between Amylose and Amylopectin components of starch.
rows.solution:
Starch is a mixture of two polymers, both built from \(\alpha\)-glucose, differing in SHAPE and in the linkages that produce it.

SHAPE AND LINKAGE. AMYLOSE is a LINEAR polymer: the glucose units are joined only by \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_4}\) glycosidic linkages, so the chain has no branches and coils into a long helix. AMYLOPECTIN is BRANCHED: it has the same \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_4}\) linkages along its chains but additional \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_6}\) linkages every twenty to twenty-five units, and each of those starts a new branch.

SOLUBILITY AND PROPORTION. AMYLOSE is water SOLUBLE and makes up about 15-20% of starch; AMYLOPECTIN is INSOLUBLE in water and makes up the remaining 80-85%.

The shape explains the solubility: the compact, heavily branched amylopectin molecule presents far less of itself to the water than the extended amylose chain does.

rows.stem:
Differentiate between :
(a) Essential amino acids and Non-essential amino acids
(b) Peptide linkage and Glycosidic linkage
(c) Fibrous protein and Globular protein
rows.solution:
(a) ESSENTIAL amino acids are those the body CANNOT synthesise for itself; they have to be supplied in the diet, and valine, leucine and lysine are among them. NON-ESSENTIAL amino acids are those the body CAN synthesise, such as glycine and alanine, so a shortage in the diet does not matter.

The names describe what the DIET must supply, not how important the acid is — both kinds are needed for protein synthesis.

(b) A PEPTIDE linkage joins two AMINO ACIDS. It is the amide bond \(-\mathrm{CO-NH}-\) formed when the carboxyl group of one condenses with the amino group of the next, losing water. It is what builds a protein.

A GLYCOSIDIC linkage joins two MONOSACCHARIDES, through an OXYGEN ATOM bridging them, again with the loss of water. It is what builds a disaccharide or a polysaccharide.

So the two differ in what they join and in the atom that does the joining — nitrogen in one case, oxygen in the other.

(c) A FIBROUS protein has its polypeptide chains running PARALLEL to one another, held side by side by hydrogen bonds and disulphide bridges, giving a thread-like structure. It is INSOLUBLE in water — keratin in hair and nail, myosin in muscle.

A GLOBULAR protein has its chain coiled and folded back on itself into a roughly SPHERICAL shape. It is SOLUBLE in water — insulin and albumin.

The functions follow from the shapes: fibrous proteins are structural material, globular ones the enzymes and hormones.
